stories.headline: Claude Haiku 5.5 lands at about 75% cheaper than Haiku 4.5, with tiered pricing that drops to $0.10 per million input tokens for prompts under 100K
stories.why_read: AI Top Story: the biggest AI thread on HN (~910 points / ~440 comments), and it's all over your timeline too. You retweeted Theo and Token Gremlin on it, and two of last night's bookmarks were about it.
body: Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5 on 7 October, calling it its cheapest, fastest and most capable small model. It's aimed at high-volume work like summaries, compaction, database queries and classification, and at running as a coding subagent under Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5. It's also the first Haiku-class model with an adjustable effort setting. Pricing is split at 100K tokens of prompt: $0.10 input and $0.50 output per million below that line, $0.50 and $2.50 above it, against $1 and $5 for Haiku 4.5. Anthropic says prompts under 100K made up around 90% of requests to the previous Haiku.

Anthropic's own table shows the jump. Haiku 5.5 scores 1620 on GDPval-AA v2.1 against 735 for Haiku 4.5, 72.4% on the OSWorld 2.1 offline subset against 15.7%, and 39.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 where Haiku 4.5 scored 0%. Sonnet 5.5 still leads on all of those. In the same post Anthropic halved Sonnet 5.5 cache-read prices, which it says makes Sonnet about 20% cheaper on most agentic work. Max 5x, Max 20x and Team subscribers also get $100, $200 and up to $500 a month in API credits.

stories.headline: Margaret Hamilton, who led the software teams that took Apollo to the Moon and helped name software engineering, has died at 90
stories.why_read: The top story on all of HN this morning (~1,640 points). Her team's priority-driven software is why Apollo 11 could land through the 1202 alarm. For anyone who ships systems for a living, she's the origin story.
body: MIT News reports that Margaret Hamilton died on 30 September at 90. She led the software engineering team at MIT's Instrumentation Lab during Apollo, heading both the Lunar Module and Command Module on-board flight software teams, which together had more than 400 people. Born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, she studied mathematics at Earlham College, came to MIT in 1959 to work on weather-prediction software with Edward Lorenz, and later became an entrepreneur and CEO. She wrote more than 130 publications and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.

Her best-known moment came minutes before the Eagle landed in July 1969, when the guidance computer raised a 1202 overload alarm. Because her team had built priority-driven software that could shed background tasks and keep mission-critical ones running, Houston trusted it and let the landing go ahead. MIT notes that she pushed early for what we'd now call defensive programming, and that she helped establish software engineering as a discipline of its own. "Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world," she said of the Apollo years.

stories.headline: OpenAI announces GPT-6 alongside an "Intelligent UI" push it says is for everyone
stories.why_read: HN (~660 points / ~370 comments) in the same news cycle as Anthropic's Haiku 5.5. It's a straight head-to-head week, and Anthropic's own Haiku chart already benchmarks against a GPT-6 variant.
body: OpenAI posted "GPT-6 and Intelligent UI for everyone". The page blocked our reader, so we're working from the headline and the discussion rather than the full post. The framing is the interesting part: the pitch centers on interface, and on availability to everyone, not on a single benchmark.

The context makes it a crowded day. Anthropic's Haiku 5.5 launch compares directly against "GPT-6 Luna", and X chatter this week has developers pairing Claude Opus 5.5 for planning with GPT-6.1 Sol for fast execution. Read the HN thread for hands-on reports before trusting any one leaderboard.

stories.headline: A day after its big math release, OpenAI withdraws three papers over a sign error and patches 14 more
stories.why_read: Follow-up to yesterday's OpenAI math story. A single sign error took down three Hodge-conjecture-adjacent papers, which is exactly the verification problem everyone was arguing about.
body: OpenAI's openai/math repository now has a history file. Its 7 October entry says a sign error in "Algebraicity of Weil classes on split abelian eightfolds" invalidates a stabilization-trace cancellation argument and the construction used by two dependent papers. All three are withdrawn, including "The rational Hodge conjecture for products of K3 surfaces". The withdrawn papers now carry notices explaining the gap, with links to the archived manuscripts.

Fourteen more manuscripts were revised with proof repairs, corrected statements and clearer hypotheses. Those include four on Lipschitz heights and Ashkin–Teller currents, six on Kähler minimal model programs and abundance, and fixes to the taming and hypersymplectic papers. The original release came with Lean formalizations of many proofs, so the useful question in the HN thread is which of the broken arguments had been formalized and which had not.

stories.headline: Musk says Starlink is being blocked in India by "certain oligarchs", and that its beams over India are switched off
stories.why_read: You retweeted three Musk posts on this last night. It's the sharpest public fight yet over Starlink's India launch, and his "beams are off" reply is a direct denial of a usage claim.
body: In a post with more than 60 million impressions, Musk wrote that SpaceX is "being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people" and called it "a crime against the people of India." In another, he argued Starlink would bring high-speed, affordable internet to people who can't afford current prices or have no connection at all.

Later he answered a claim that Starlink had been used inside India: "Starlink beams are turned off over India, so the claim that they were used by anyone for any reason is absolutely false." He didn't name anyone, and the posts don't say what is holding up the service. Treat this as one side of a regulatory and commercial fight that is still playing out.

stories.headline: An LLM-written Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, checker and LSP: $400K of OpenAI tokens stalled at 84%, then Opus 5.5 restarted from scratch for about $24K
stories.why_read: HN (~110 comments): the most concrete agent-vs-agent cost story of the week, with real token bills and a big caveat from the author, who says he has never read a line of the code.
body: pingdotgg's ts-rust (published as tsc-rs) is an attempt to see whether LLMs can port the TypeScript compiler, type checker and language server to Rust. The README says the first pass used more than $400,000 in API-priced tokens with GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra. Over months of loops, those models wrote more than 1.3 million lines of Rust and never got past about 84% compatibility.

Then Opus 5.5 was given the job and started over. It had a working v0 in 10 hours, and total spend came to about $24,047 over two weeks, run through Claude subscriptions. The author claims 100% compatibility on every real-world project tested so far, but calls it an early release with known problems. Everything past the README's "slop line" was written by the models, so read it as a capability demo and benchmark carefully before you depend on it.

stories.headline: Musk says there's "ZERO doubt" Tesla and SpaceX will build and run the Terafab chip plants in Austin; TSMC could only sublease
stories.why_read: Chips plus your home turf: two Austin fabs aimed at more than a terawatt of AI compute, with Intel's 14A process still in the picture.
body: According to X News summaries, Musk said Tesla and SpaceX will fully own and operate two Terafab factories in Austin. One would serve Tesla vehicles and Optimus robots, and the other AI data centers and SpaceX. The stated target is more than one terawatt of AI compute capacity. Earlier comments about talks with TSMC had pushed TSMC shares to records and knocked Intel down.

His clarification is that TSMC might sublease space at most, with no operating role, while Intel stays on as a development partner using its 14A process. Intel shares reportedly rebounded on that. Nothing here is a signed deal yet, so watch for filings and site work rather than posts.

stories.headline: The 9th State of AI Report is out: Claude led 26% of Anthropic's measured model R&D work in August, up from under 1% in February
stories.why_read: Nathan Benaich's annual deck is the best single map of the year in AI research, industry and policy. This year's theme is AI that helps build AI, and the world-model work matters for robotaxis.
body: Air Street Capital's Nathan Benaich published the 2026 State of AI Report, a 244-slide deck covering research, industry, safety and politics. Its opening argument is that AI is already speeding up AI development. It cites Anthropic's internal index showing Claude led 26% of measured model R&D work in August, with researchers setting and supervising the tasks, up from under 1% in February.

It also covers world models as a training route for physical AI, including Wayve's GAIA-4, which turns recorded driving scenes into simulations where an AI driver's steering and braking change what it sees next. The report grades its past predictions too. It cites its call that an open-source model would pass OpenAI's o1, which DeepSeek-R1 then did.

stories.headline: Docker ships docker-agent, a CLI plugin for declarative multi-agent teams in YAML with MCP tools and OCI packaging
stories.why_read: HN (~250 points): agents defined as versionable YAML and shipped through any OCI registry. That's very much your enterprise DevOps world.
body: docker-agent runs as `docker agent` and lets you define agents, their models and toolsets in a YAML file, then run them with one command. It supports multi-agent teams that delegate to each other, built-in think, todo and memory tools, and any MCP server, whether local, remote or Docker-based. Retrieval is pluggable, with BM25, embeddings, hybrid search and reranking.

It's provider-agnostic, covering OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, Mistral, xAI and Docker Model Runner. Agents can be pushed to and pulled from OCI registries like container images. It ships preinstalled in Docker Desktop 4.63 and later, and is also on Homebrew.

stories.headline: Chrome 155 ships JPEG XL decoding, through a new memory-safe decoder written in Rust
stories.why_read: HN (~550 points): a long-running web standards saga ends, and the security story (a Rust decoder in the renderer) is the systems angle.
body: Google's Chrome team says JPEG XL decoding ships starting in Chrome 155. The format offers 30–50% better compression than JPEG, lossless compression, built-in HDR, and lossless transcoding of existing JPEGs. Google suggests trying both AVIF and JPEG XL, and expects JPEG XL to help most with high-fidelity or lossless photos and fine-grained progressive decoding.

The notable engineering choice is jxl-rs, a Rust reimplementation of the decoder. The post argues that image decoders handle untrusted binary data from the network inside the renderer, which makes them prime attack surface, and that memory safety had to come first. It also covers the performance work it took to make the Rust decoder fast.

stories.headline: The first thorium-229 nuclear clocks begin ticking in Vienna and Beijing
stories.why_read: Physics for your pinned-post list: clocks that tick on a nuclear transition rather than an electron's could beat today's atomic clocks.
body: The New York Times reports that labs in Vienna and Beijing have the first nuclear clocks running, based on the thorium-229 nucleus. Our reader couldn't get past the paywall, so we're working from the headline and the HN thread rather than the article.

The idea behind these clocks is that a transition inside an atomic nucleus is much better shielded from outside noise than the electron transitions today's atomic clocks use. That could mean more stable timekeeping and new tests of whether fundamental constants drift.

stories.headline: Scientists sequence the genome of Jonathan, the 194-year-old tortoise who is the oldest land animal alive
stories.why_read: Science and human interest in one. He hatched around 1832, before Darwin's Origin of Species, and his genome is now a longevity dataset.
body: 404 Media's Becky Ferreira reports on a study published Wednesday in Science Advances. It sequenced, for the first time, the genome of Jonathan, an Aldabra giant tortoise on Saint Helena. He hatched around 1832 in the Seychelles and was taken to Saint Helena in the 1880s as a gift to the British governor. He has lived there ever since.

Aldabra tortoises often pass 100, but Jonathan is an outlier even for his species. The researchers are looking at his genome for clues to extreme longevity that might eventually inform human aging research.

stories.headline: Remembering Nana Patekar, who won three National Film Awards and served in the Territorial Army through Kargil
stories.why_read: You retweeted this tribute last night. It's a reminder of an actor whose public life went well beyond the screen.
body: A widely shared tribute marking Nana Patekar's death notes that he won three National Film Awards and four Filmfare Awards and received the Padma Shri in 2013. It also notes that he served in the Indian Territorial Army from 1990 to 2013, retiring as an Honorary Lieutenant Colonel, and took part in the 1999 Kargil War.
This comes from a fan tribute post rather than an official obituary, so check a news report for the full details.

stories.headline: Dirty Tesla on a fresh Cybercab ride: "even better than I remember"
stories.why_read: One of your retweets last night, posted with ride video. Pair it with Phil Duan's line that manual driving is now like hand-coding Perl, which you also retweeted.
body: Dirty Tesla posted a new Cybercab ride video with the line "Cybercab is even better than I remember. What an amazing product." It comes as X News summaries describe roughly 200 steering-wheel-free Cybercabs gathering at a Houston fleet lot ahead of an expansion beyond Austin.

You also retweeted Phil Duan: "Manual driving is like riding a horse or hand-coding in Perl and PHP. You can still do it. You just don't have to." A Dirty Tesla post in last night's bookmarks made a similar point about letting FSD do its thing.

stories.headline: Starship 40 arrives at the Port of Brownsville after its trip home
stories.why_read: From your Starship retweets: a photo of a flown ship coming back to Texas by sea.
body: Starship Gazer posted photos on 7 October of Starship 40 arriving at the Port of Brownsville "after completing an epic journey." The post got about 2,800 likes.
It lands next to this week's Gigabay chatter about building and refurbishing up to 1,000 Starships a year at Starbase. Watching hardware come home is a reminder that reuse is the whole plan.

stories.headline: What's new in Grok Bot: engineering updates, Google connectors, Team Bots in Slack and voice calls
stories.why_read: From your bookmarks and retweets: the release walkthrough, plus a user saying Grok Bot caught legal-file gaps that Claude and ChatGPT missed.
body: @mattyp's walkthrough video, which you bookmarked, covers the main bot, engineering updates, knowledge work and Google connectors, Team Bots in Slack, Team Bot voice calls and status lines, and plugin search with Command K. @mikepat711's bookmarked X article explains how he uses Grok Bot as the one front door that drives his Claude and Grok Build subscriptions.

You also retweeted @iruletheworldmo, who says he gave Grok Bot access to six months of legal files he'd been working through with Claude and ChatGPT. He says it immediately spotted gaps and misfiled errors his team and earlier AI checks had missed. That's one user's account, but it's a striking one.

stories.headline: good-css: 47 modern CSS techniques your coding agent will reach for first
stories.why_read: You retweeted it, and about 1,600 people bookmarked it. It's a neat fix for agents that know :has(), subgrid and anchor positioning but never use them.
body: Vojta Holik's point is that coding agents know modern CSS like :has(), subgrid and anchor positioning, but rarely reach for them. good-css packages 47 modern CSS techniques so the agent tries them first.
It's part of a growing pattern of small, opinionated skill packs that steer an agent's defaults rather than trying to change the model.

stories.headline: ISO-GLOW: a Claude skill that turns a description into a glowing, clickable isometric drawing in one HTML file
stories.why_read: A fun retweet from last night. Describe a device or building, and you get back a single interactive HTML file.
body: April packaged her isometric-drawing workflow as a Claude skill. Describe an object, device or building, and ISO-GLOW returns one HTML file with a fine-line isometric drawing where whatever is switched on glows and each part you press does something.
The site has a one-line install into ~/.claude/skills and a gallery of examples, each made from a single request. The post has about 2,200 bookmarks.

stories.headline: Nvidia is reportedly in talks to put another $1 billion into humanoid-robot maker Figure
stories.why_read: Nvidia and physical AI: a planned cluster of up to 100,000 Vera Rubin GPUs in Barstow, Texas, is part of the story.
body: According to X News summaries of reports, Nvidia is in talks to invest about $1 billion more in Figure AI, building on its stake from Figure's Series C and its role supplying hardware for Figure's Helix models.

Figure plans a compute cluster of up to 100,000 Nvidia Vera Rubin GPUs in Barstow, Texas, starting in 2027, with an initial $3.5 billion commitment that could top $6 billion. Jensen Huang frames it as a "robotics flywheel" for training, simulating and deploying robots.

stories.headline: White House to award the National Medal of Science to Musk, Huang, Brin and Lisa Su today
stories.why_read: Today's ceremony puts the people behind rockets, EVs and AI chips on the same stage.
body: X News summaries say the White House will present the National Medal of Science on Thursday to Elon Musk, Sergey Brin, Jensen Huang and Lisa Su at a summit titled "Science: A New Golden Age." Michael Dell and Satya Nadella are set to receive the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.
A White House spokesperson credited the recipients with driving U.S. innovation in rockets, EVs and AI.

stories.headline: IonQ reaches Stage C of DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative
stories.why_read: Physics with a deadline: independent testing through 2029 of whether trapped-ion machines can scale to fault tolerance.
body: Per X News summaries, IonQ has advanced to Stage C, the final testing phase of DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, under a potential agreement worth up to $300 million. Independent evaluators will check whether its trapped-ion Superion systems can deliver large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing and be manufactured reliably.
IonQ joins IBM, Atom Computing and Diraq at this stage. The company is aiming for utility-scale quantum computing by 2033.

stories.headline: A $1.8 billion Virtual Biology Initiative aims to build open, AI-ready datasets of how cells respond
stories.why_read: Science plus AI: the DOE, NIH, DeepMind, Meta and Isomorphic Labs are pooling effort on data, not models.
body: X News summaries say the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub, U.S. agencies including the Department of Energy and NIH, Google DeepMind, Meta and Isomorphic Labs have launched an expanded $1.8 billion Virtual Biology Initiative. It will use tools such as cryo-electron tomography to build standardized datasets for modeling how cells respond to drugs and disease.
The data is to be released openly after a short embargo, with a first release expected in about a year.

stories.headline: Chinese open models led OpenRouter traffic in late September, with DeepSeek alone at 36.8 trillion tokens
stories.why_read: Open-source LLM signal: on at least one big router, price-performance is beating brand names.
body: X News summaries report that Chinese models dominated OpenRouter, the API router that fronts hundreds of model providers, in late September. DeepSeek alone processed 36.8 trillion tokens in a week, more than OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and SpaceXAI models combined on that platform.
The caveat is that OpenRouter is a slice of total AI traffic, not all of it. Still, it's a real-world read on what cost-conscious developers pick for coding and bulk work.

stories.headline: How machines learned precision: from Maudslay's screw-cutting lathe to straight rails and even threads
stories.why_read: HN (~180 points): an illustrated history for a mechanical engineer. Machines had to get accurate before they could make anything else accurate.
body: This interactive essay starts with the kind of screw-cutting lathe Henry Maudslay built in London around 1800, a carriage moved by a lead screw along straight iron rails. The catch is that the lathe's own parts have to be accurate first. A bent rail or an unevenly pitched screw copies its error into everything it makes, which is how you get leaking pistons, wobbling shafts and jammed nuts.
It walks through how 18th- and 19th-century workshops bootstrapped flatness, straightness and even threads. That bootstrapping is the base layer under every machine tool, and so under every chip fab.

stories.headline: Push ifs up and fors down: the TigerBeetle idiom, its algebra, and where it breaks
stories.why_read: HN (~155 points): a practical refactoring rule from TigerBeetle's Tiger Style, worked through carefully.
body: The post starts from TigerBeetle's Tiger Style advice: centralize control flow by keeping switch and if statements in the parent function, and move non-branching logic into helpers. Batch work goes down into loops that process many items at once.
He then formalizes why this works and maps out where the idiom stops helping. It's useful for anyone reviewing agent-written code that scatters branching everywhere.

stories.headline: A minimal kernel written in Swift, booting in QEMU
stories.why_read: HN: close-to-the-metal fun. Swift can now get close enough to the metal for a toy kernel.
body: The author writes up a small experiment in writing a very basic kernel in Swift and running it on QEMU. The goal isn't to replace anything, just to see how far Swift can go at that level.
A September update switched to Swift's new @c attribute, which formalizes @_cdecl for exposing Swift functions as C, after a tip from Max Desiatov.

stories.headline: Terence Tao: "Math 2.0" will have to value progress beyond being first to solve a problem
stories.why_read: HN (~345 points): the most thoughtful response to this week's flood of AI-produced proofs, from the mathematician people listen to most.
body: Ending a four-part Mathstodon thread, Tao argues that "Math 1.0" placed a premium on being first to solve an open problem, and that this goal has now been optimized "to the point of unsustainability." Math 2.0, he says, will need to value exposition, community building and opening new directions, not just raw problem solving.

He thinks AI can help with all of those, but only with more imagination than pointing an agent at a list of open problems. He also says the field will need to rethink its criteria for education, publication and career advancement.

stories.headline: Scott Aaronson on the "Mathocalypse": 372 AI-produced results, including a claimed proof of the Unique Games Conjecture
stories.why_read: HN (~270 points / ~290 comments): a UT Austin professor's very human reaction, since his wife's career problem was on the list.
body: Aaronson calls the OpenAI release "surely one of the biggest days in mathematical history." He writes that its 372 results include a proof of Subhash Khot's Unique Games Conjecture, which his wife, complexity theorist Dana Moshkovitz, has worked toward for years. He opens with his 9-year-old taunting her that a robot solved her problem.
Read it alongside today's withdrawals of three OpenAI papers and Tao's thread. Together they show the field moving between awe and verification in real time.

stories.headline: "Navier–Stokes lost in translation": why Lean-checking an AI's autoformalization doesn't certify the original proof
stories.why_read: HN (~315 points): a sharp argument that a green Lean check can certify the wrong statement.
body: Alexander Bastounis, Fabian Circelli and Anders C. Hansen take aim at autoformalization, where an AI translates a natural-language proof into Lean and the Lean version is checked mechanically. They cite OpenAI's announced Navier–Stokes blow-up proof and argue the translation step can give no confidence in the original argument.

Their claim is that resolving ambiguity in mathematical prose, which a faithful translation requires, sits arbitrarily high in the Solvability Complexity Index hierarchy. Informally, they say faithful autoformalization is harder than any computational problem, including the halting problem.

stories.headline: 1920s photos of workers dwarfed by giant generators spark a thread on building the electrical age
stories.why_read: Energy history for your pinned post: the grid build-out was the AI data-center race of its day.
body: X News summaries say David Holz shared black-and-white photos of 1920s crews on scaffolding inside towering generator stator assemblies lined with thousands of coils. Engineers replied with modern shots from atop 200-megawatt hydro units.

Commenters pointed to milestones like General Electric's record 208,000-kilowatt turbo-generator for Chicago's State Line plant in 1929. They drew the obvious parallel to today's compute and power build-outs, which are still built at human scale.
